• From the Betta splendens complex. IUCN Red List: N/A.
  • Smaragdina are identified by the snake-like scales that cover their opercular membrane and body.
  • Noted to be hardy and able to withstand low temperature due to their high elevation habitat.
  • Body: slender and elongated, streamlined and slightly compressed. Maximum standard length about 2.8 inches (7 cm); the page also lists max size as 2.3 inches.
  • Tail: typically rounded or spadetail, with long fins featuring a distinctive spider web-like pattern of black transverse bars between caudal rays.
  • Coloration: dark brown to black body with iridescent green or blue scales. Males display vibrant green-blue hues and red fin accents, while females are duller with brownish tones and muted iridescence.
  • Operculum: black with a "snake-scale" pattern of iridescent green or blue scales in males, more pronounced during flaring. Females have less vivid, simpler markings.

Only healthy, high quality fish are selected for shipping. All fish go through 2 or more weeks of quarantine before being sold, including medication to remove parasites such as velvet and ich. All males come from the same lineage and are generally similar. Be sure to have the habitat ready before purchase.
Native to northeastern Thailand, specifically around Bueng Khong Long Lake in Bueng Kan province.

Inhabits slow-moving, shallow waters like rice paddies, swamps, and streams with dense vegetation and low oxygen. Prefers warm (25-27°C), slightly acidic (pH 5-7) water, using its labyrinth organ for breathing.

• TDS: 60 - 200 (kept in soft water with low TDS to match other wild bettas, but they are more tolerant of water conditions).
  • pH: 5.0-7.0
  • Temperature: 75-85°F (much better coloration at warmer temperature above 78°F). Known to be able to withstand very low temperature (60°F).
Carnivorous. Currently fed live blackworms, frozen bloodworms and pellets.
Males are VERY aggressive and should be kept alone or in tanks with non-male betta mates. Can be kept in a planted community tank of multiple females if there is adequate space.
Males display vibrant green-blue hues and red fin accents, while females are duller with brownish tones and muted iridescence. Females have less vivid, simpler operculum markings.
